# Block 8: AI-assisted code review {.unnumbered} :::{.callout-note} **Prerequisite.** This block uses the project folder from (`ANALYSIS.R` and its data files) and the twelve problems, P1–P12, that you catalogued in the [manual code-review chapter](07-code-review.qmd). That catalogue is the answer key you will use to grade the AI. If you have not completed that chapter, your instructor will give you the answer key after Part 3; do not look at it before you have run your review. ::: :::{.callout-note} **The framing for this session.** The [manual code-review chapter](07-code-review.qmd) argued that the *Reliable* question (does the code do what the analyst intended?) is one that no tool can answer for you. This block does not retract that. It asks a narrower question: where is an AI reviewer useful, and can you tell when it is wrong? You are reviewing a script whose problems you already know, so you can grade the machine rather than trust it. ::: *⏱ ~90 minutes* ## Part 1: What AI is, and is not, good for in code review {#ai-why} *⏱ ~15 minutes* The appeal of an AI reviewer is speed and coverage: it reads every line and does not tire. The danger is fluent, confident output that is sometimes wrong, in the same tone whether it is right or wrong. Map its likely strengths onto the four Rs of code review (Ivimey-Cook et al., 2023): ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
AI capability mapped onto the four Rs
R AI is likely to be... Why
Reported Useful for drafting It can summarise what the script appears to do and flag missing documentation or undocumented exclusions. It cannot know the intended analysis unless you state it.
Run Strong, if it can execute An agent that runs the script in a fresh R session can show whether it runs. A chat window can only predict, and its prediction can read as though it ran the code.
Reliable Weak Silent semantic errors (P4 precedence, P8 sentinel, P9 incomparable models, P10 wrong family) depend on context. Expect some caught, some missed and some invented, all in the same confident tone.
Reproducible Mixed It can flag a missing lockfile or session record. It can confirm that results reproduce only by running the code and comparing outputs.
````` ::: ::: **What the evidence says, and does not say.** In an industrial study of an LLM-based review tool, about three-quarters of the automated comments were marked as resolved by developers, and most practitioners reported only a minor improvement in code quality (Cihan et al., 2025). A companion experiment by the same group found that review performance dropped when the model was not given a description of what the code was meant to do (Cihan, 2025, master's thesis). Both studies concern software engineering, not statistical analysis scripts. No study we know of measures AI review of analysis code like `ANALYSIS.R`, which is why you will measure it yourself in Part 3. The practical rule: **treat every AI finding as a claim to verify, and treat the absence of a finding as no evidence that the problem is absent.** :::{.callout-tip} **Opening poll** *(type in chat)* "If an AI code reviewer told you your analysis was clean, would you trust it enough to submit?" A: Yes, it read every line B: Only if I had also read it myself C: No, I would trust my own review over the AI's D: I would trust it for *Run*, not for *Reliable* Keep the result visible; we return to it at the end. ::: ## Part 2: Telling the AI how to behave {#ai-prompting} *⏱ ~20 minutes* A vague prompt ("review my code") tends to produce a vague, generous review. Give the AI the same scaffold you used in the manual review. ### The four things a review prompt should contain 1. **A role and a standard.** For example: "You are a critical code reviewer for an ecology journal applying the four Rs (Reported, Run, Reliable, Reproducible)." This gives the output a structure you can check. 2. **The intended analysis.** The AI cannot judge *Reported* or *Reliable* without knowing what the code is meant to do. State the model from the OSF page: `TO ~ strain * diet + (1 | B)`, where `TO` is a count. Without this, it cannot know that a Gaussian `lmer()` is the wrong family (P10). 3. **An instruction against flattery.** "Do not praise. For each issue give the line number, the R it violates, the severity, and a concrete fix." Check the output for praise anyway; the instruction is a request. 4. **A demand for honest uncertainty.** "Flag anything you cannot determine by reading alone as NEEDS HUMAN CHECK, rather than guessing." :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} **Activity: write the review prompt (10 minutes)** :::: ::::{.task-container} Write a prompt containing all four elements. The room splits in two for a controlled comparison: - **Group A** includes the line about the 9999 sentinel in the skeleton below. - **Group B** deletes it. Everything else stays the same.
``` You are a critical code reviewer for an evolutionary-biology journal. Review ANALYSIS.R using the four Rs: Reported, Run, Reliable, Reproducible. The intended analysis (from the pre-registration) is: total offspring (TO, a count: non-negative integer, often overdispersed) modelled as TO ~ strain * diet + (1 | block), with block as a random effect. Rules: - Do NOT praise the code. Report only problems. - For each issue: line number(s), which R it violates, severity (critical / high / medium), and a concrete one-line fix. - The raw data use 9999 as a "not recorded" code. Check whether this is handled. <- Group B: delete this line - Flag anything you CANNOT determine by reading alone as "NEEDS HUMAN CHECK" rather than guessing. - If you are uncertain about a finding, say so explicitly. Organise your output by the four Rs. ```
:::: ::: ## Part 3: Running the review {#ai-running} *⏱ ~35 minutes* ### Path A: a local agent, read-only Use Claude Code in `plan` mode, Posit Assistant in Ask mode, or Copilot Chat in Ask. At this rung the agent can read every file in the project but cannot change any, which is what a review needs. 1. Open the whole OSF project folder, so the agent can see the data files as well as `ANALYSIS.R`. 2. Give it your Part 2 prompt. 3. Save its review to a file of your own before moving on. ### Path A, step 2: let it run the script (optional) An agent that can execute R can turn the *Run* question from a prediction into evidence. Switch to rung 3 (acting with approval) and ask: ``` Run ANALYSIS.R from a fresh R session with Rscript and report the exact output and any errors. Do not install packages; if a package is missing, report which one. Do not edit any file. ``` Read the approval prompt before approving the command, and read the output it reports. If it says "the script runs", find the command it ran and the output it saw. A claim that the script runs, with no command and no output, is a prediction. Missing packages on your machine are a finding about the environment, not about the code. ### Path B: chat window If you have no agent, paste the whole of `ANALYSIS.R` into any chat window, followed by your Part 2 prompt. :::{.callout-warning} **The chat window's failure mode.** A chat window cannot run anything. Asked "does this code run?", it will produce a fluent answer that can read as though it executed the code. It did not. Ask instead "what would *prevent* this running?", and treat any claim about reproduced results as unsupported. ::: ### Path C: Copilot code review on a pull request (demonstration) If your repository is on GitHub, open a pull request containing `ANALYSIS.R` and request Copilot as a reviewer. Its comments appear on the changed lines, like a colleague's. It reads the repository's custom instructions, so the review conventions you wrote in the [instructions-and-skills block](11e-instructions-skills.qmd) apply. :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} **Activity: grade the machine (20 minutes)** :::: ::::{.task-container} Open your P1–P12 catalogue beside the AI's review and score it: - **Hits:** which of P1–P12 did it identify correctly? - **Misses:** which did it miss? Look especially at P4 (precedence) and P8 (sentinel), the silent, consequential ones. - **False positives:** what did it flag that is not a real problem, or describe wrongly? - **Execution claims:** did it claim the script runs or reproduces? On what evidence? Post your group (A or B), your hit count, your most consequential miss and your most confident false positive in the chat, with line numbers. :::: ::: :::{.callout-note} **Debrief (5 minutes)** 1. Compare P8 hit rates between Group A and Group B. The script alone does not reveal that 9999 is a code; the data and your knowledge do. What does that say about reviewing code without the data? 2. Whose AI produced the most confident false positive? A missed bug you may catch later; a fabricated one wastes review time and erodes trust in the tool. 3. Did any agent claim the script runs without having run it? 4. Return to the opening poll. Would you change your answer? ::: ## Part 4: Generating the README with AI {#ai-readme} *⏱ ~20 minutes* The second deliverable is the documentation that makes *Reported* and *Run* answerable: a README. You are provided with the `research-readme` skill: a `SKILL.md`, two helper scripts and a template. You run this in two passes. The first shows the failure; the second shows the fix. ### Pass 1: README from the AI alone (demonstration, ~4 minutes) Give the AI only `ANALYSIS.R` and the data, and ask for a README with no constraints. The result reads as complete. It will assign plausible units, describe variables it cannot have verified, and may state package versions it has no way to know. Note what it asserts about the variables and dependencies; Pass 2 replaces each guess with a fact you generate. ### Pass 2: README from verifiable inputs The skill's rules are that the AI must **not fabricate metadata**, and that automatic summaries **describe; they do not interpret**. So you generate the facts mechanically, and the AI only assembles and phrases them. #### Step 1: Generate the inputs yourself (R, not AI) ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} skill_dir <- here::here(".agents", "skills", "research-readme", "scripts") source(file.path(skill_dir, "describe_csv.R")) describe_project_csvs(here::here()) # type, missing count and range per column source(file.path(skill_dir, "scan_packages.R")) print_lockfile(here::here("renv.lock")) # R and package versions, or a finding ``` ::: This project has no `renv.lock`. `scan_packages.R` reports that as an explicit finding rather than an error, and the README must say so. You cannot pin versions you never recorded. Look at the offspring column in the summary: its range will read something like `2 to 9999`. The 9999 code (P8) is a real number in the file, and the summary reports it without judgement. Judging plausibility is your job. That honest, uninterpreted range is the visible trace of the sentinel. #### Step 2: Hand the AI the specification and the inputs **Agent path:** invoke `/research-readme` and let its five stages run. It will ask you for what it cannot find. **Chat path:** paste the structure from `references/readme_template.md` and the output you just generated, with this prompt: ``` Draft a research README.md for this analysis repository, using exactly the sections in the template I paste below, in order. Use ONLY the facts I provide. Do not invent DOIs, ORCIDs, units or package versions. Where a value is missing, insert a visible placeholder: Per-column summaries: [paste describe_project_csvs() output] Dependencies: [paste print_lockfile() output] Run order: 01_data_cleaning.R, then 02_analysis.R. Add an AI declaration stating that an AI assisted in drafting this README, naming the model and today's date. Make no claims about AI use elsewhere. ``` :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} **Activity: audit the README (10 minutes)** :::: ::::{.task-container} Audit the draft against three of the skill's rules: 1. **No fabrication.** Pick three facts. Can you trace each to an input you gave? If not, it is invented. 2. **Describe, do not interpret.** Did the AI assign units or meanings you did not supply? Did the `2 to 9999` range survive, or was it "tidied" into something plausible and wrong? 3. **README only.** Confirm with `git status` that nothing except `README.md` changed. Post the worst fabrication or interpretation you caught, and say whether the README's offspring range alone would have led you back to P8. :::: ::: ### The skill bundle The bundle is reproduced here for reference; you do not edit it during the session. It lives in `.agents/skills/research-readme/`, linked into `.claude/skills/` for Claude Code as described in the [instructions-and-skills block](11e-instructions-skills.qmd). ``` research-readme/ ├── SKILL.md ├── scripts/ │ ├── describe_csv.R │ └── scan_packages.R └── references/ └── readme_template.md ``` :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ### `scripts/describe_csv.R` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # describe_csv.R ---- # Purpose: one row per column of a CSV file: name, the type readr assigns, # missing-value count, and a brief range (numeric) or distinct-value count # (other). Describes; does not interpret. # Used by: research-readme skill, Stage 2. describe_range <- function(x) { if (all(is.na(x))) { return("all values missing") } if (is.numeric(x)) { return(paste(min(x, na.rm = TRUE), "to", max(x, na.rm = TRUE))) } paste(dplyr::n_distinct(x, na.rm = TRUE), "distinct values") } # one-row-per-column summary of a single CSV ---- describe_csv <- function(path) { stopifnot(is.character(path), length(path) == 1L, file.exists(path)) data_df <- readr::read_csv(path, show_col_types = FALSE) tibble::tibble( file = basename(path), column = names(data_df), type = purrr::map_chr(data_df, \(x) class(x)[1]), n_missing = purrr::map_int(data_df, \(x) sum(is.na(x))), range = purrr::map_chr(data_df, describe_range), # completed by the user during Stage 2: description = NA_character_, unit = NA_character_ ) } # describe every CSV in a project, skipping renv and git folders ---- describe_project_csvs <- function(project_dir) { stopifnot(dir.exists(project_dir)) csv_paths <- list.files( project_dir, pattern = "\\.csv$", recursive = TRUE, full.names = TRUE, ignore.case = TRUE ) csv_paths <- csv_paths[!grepl("(^|/)(renv|\\.git)/", csv_paths)] if (length(csv_paths) == 0L) { message("No CSV files found under ", project_dir) return(tibble::tibble()) } csv_paths |> purrr::map(describe_csv) |> purrr::list_rbind() } ``` ::: ::: :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ### `scripts/scan_packages.R` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # scan_packages.R ---- # Purpose: read renv.lock and report the R version and pinned package # versions. A missing lockfile is reported as a finding, not an error. # Used by: research-readme skill, Stage 4. read_lockfile <- function(lock_path = "renv.lock") { if (!file.exists(lock_path)) { return(list(found = FALSE, r_version = NA_character_, packages = tibble::tibble())) } lock <- jsonlite::read_json(lock_path) packages <- purrr::pluck(lock, "Packages", .default = list()) packages_df <- tibble::tibble( package = unname(purrr::map_chr(packages, \(p) purrr::pluck(p, "Package", .default = NA_character_))), version = unname(purrr::map_chr(packages, \(p) purrr::pluck(p, "Version", .default = NA_character_))) ) |> dplyr::arrange(package) list( found = TRUE, r_version = purrr::pluck(lock, "R", "Version", .default = NA_character_), packages = packages_df ) } print_lockfile <- function(lock_path = "renv.lock") { info <- read_lockfile(lock_path) if (!info$found) { cat( "No lockfile found at ", lock_path, ".\n", "FINDING: package versions were not recorded.\n", "README text: \n", sep = "" ) return(invisible(info)) } cat("R version: ", info$r_version, "\n\n", sep = "") print(info$packages, n = Inf) invisible(info) } ``` ::: ::: :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ### `SKILL.md` ```markdown --- name: research-readme description: >- Writes a README.md for a research repository whose code and data accompany a paper. Use when asked to write a README for an analysis project, document a repository for a paper, or prepare code for journal submission or archiving (Zenodo, Figshare, OSF). Not for general software READMEs and not for auditing code. disable-model-invocation: true --- # Research README generator Produces one README.md for a repository of R code and data that accompanies a manuscript, including the metadata that journals and archives expect: persistent identifiers, ORCIDs, funding, per-variable descriptions with units, an explicit script run order, and a dependency record. ## Operating constraints These hold for the whole conversation unless the user explicitly withdraws them. 1. The only file you create or overwrite is README.md. Do not edit, rename or delete any other file. If you notice an apparent error in code or data, record it under "Open questions" in the README or report it in chat, and leave the file untouched. 2. Do not fabricate metadata. DOIs, ORCIDs, grant numbers, collection dates, units and affiliations come from the user or from a file the user points to. If a value is unknown, insert a placeholder (see Placeholders). 3. Automatic summaries describe; they do not interpret. Report column type, missing count and range. Do not state what a variable means, its unit, or whether a value is plausible. 4. Work conversationally and write the file directly; do not build an app. ## Before executing Present a short numbered plan: the folder to be scanned, that only README.md will be written, and the five stages below. Wait for the user to confirm. ## Stage 1: Project information Collect title, abstract, DOIs (paper; archived code and data), licences, authors with ORCIDs and affiliations, and funders with grant numbers. Read these from CITATION.cff, codemeta.json or DESCRIPTION if present, and ask only for what is missing. Pair each author with their own ORCID and affiliation. If no code licence is supplied, flag it prominently and use a placeholder; do not choose a licence for the user. ## Stage 2: Files and variable summaries List the data and code files. For CSV files, run describe_project_csvs() from scripts/describe_csv.R and use its output as a scaffold. Ask the user for each column's description and unit, and for collection dates and locations per data file. List other tabular formats (.xlsx, .tsv) and ask the user to describe their columns by hand. Never infer units from column names. ## Stage 3: Script order List executable files (.R, .Rmd, .qmd). Propose a run order using numeric prefixes (01_, 02_) as the first signal, and ask the user to confirm or reorder; the user's order is authoritative. Collect a one-line description of each script. Do not run any script to determine the order. ## Stage 4: R packages and versions Run print_lockfile() from scripts/scan_packages.R. - If a lockfile exists, the Dependencies section states the R version, says that versions are pinned in renv.lock, gives the restore command renv::restore(), and includes the package table. - If no lockfile exists, the Dependencies section states that package versions were not recorded, and contains the placeholder from print_lockfile(). Do not guess versions or scan the installed library. ## Stage 5: Assemble, preview and reader-test Fill references/readme_template.md. Show the rendered Markdown in chat. Then read it as a newcomer who has only the repository and the paper: could they find the data, restore the environment, run the scripts in order and understand every variable? List any section still holding a placeholder. On confirmation, write README.md to the project root. ## AI declaration State that an AI assisted in generating this README, naming the model if the user wishes, with the date. Make no claims about AI use elsewhere in the project unless the user states them, and then record exactly what they state. ## Placeholders Write every unknown value as a visible placeholder, in exactly this form: Flag a missing code licence and a missing code or data DOI as blocking for submission, but still write the file so the user has a working draft. ## Scope This skill does not audit code quality or reproducibility, and does not produce figures. If asked to do either mid-run, say so and stop that part of the request. ## References - Ivimey-Cook, E.R. et al. (2023) Implementing code review in the scientific workflow. Journal of Evolutionary Biology 36(10), 1347–1356. - Ivimey-Cook, E.R. et al. (2025) TADA! Simple guidelines to improve analytical code sharing for transparency and reproducibility. EcoEvoRxiv. ``` ::: :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ### `references/readme_template.md` The Dependencies section is a single token, filled with one of the two versions defined in Stage 4 of `SKILL.md`, so the README is accurate whether or not a lockfile exists. ```markdown # {{TITLE}} {{DOI_BADGE}} {{LICENCE_BADGE}} ## Description {{DESCRIPTION}} ## Abstract {{ABSTRACT}} ## Instructions This repository contains the code and data accompanying the manuscript above. To reproduce the analysis: 1. Obtain the data as described under *Data files*. 2. Set up the R environment as described under *Dependencies*. 3. Run the scripts in the order given under *Scripts*. ## Authors | Name | ORCID | Affiliation | |------|-------|-------------| {{AUTHOR_ROWS}} ### Funding {{FUNDING}} ## Data files {{PER_FILE_SECTIONS}} ## Scripts Run in this order: | Order | Script | Description | |-------|--------|-------------| {{SCRIPT_ROWS}} ## Dependencies {{DEPENDENCIES}} ## Open questions {{OPEN_QUESTIONS}} ## AI declaration {{AI_DECLARATION}} ``` ::: ## Check your understanding **An AI reviewer reports that `ANALYSIS.R` "runs without errors". What do you need before treating that as evidence?**
**Why did Group A catch P8 more often than Group B?**
## Glossary ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Term Definition
Agent An AI that can read across a project's files and, depending on its mode, edit them and run commands, as opposed to a chat window that sees only pasted text
Read-only rung A mode in which the assistant can read but not change anything: Claude Code plan mode, Posit Assistant Ask mode, Copilot Ask
False positive (in review) A problem the AI reports confidently that is not real, or is described wrongly
Claimed execution A statement that code runs or reproduces, made without a command and its output to support it
Sentinel value A number with a special meaning (9999 = not recorded); detectable from the data or from your instruction, not from the code alone
AI declaration A README statement recording that an AI assisted, naming the model and date, and making no claims about AI use elsewhere
````` ::: ::: ## Reading - **Ivimey-Cook, E.R., et al. (2023).** Implementing code review in the scientific workflow: insights from ecology and evolutionary biology. *Journal of Evolutionary Biology*, 36(10), 1347–1356. - **Ivimey-Cook, E.R., et al. (2025).** TADA! Simple guidelines to improve analytical code sharing for transparency and reproducibility. *EcoEvoRxiv* (preprint). - **Cihan, U., Haratian, V., İçöz, A., et al. (2025).** Automated code review in practice. *Proceedings of the 47th International Conference on Software Engineering: Software Engineering in Practice (ICSE-SEIP)*, 425–436. - **Cihan, U. (2025).** *Automated code review: empirical evidence from experiments and industry*. Master's thesis, Bilkent University. - **Course OSF page:**
